Dictionary Expansion for Incompletely Overlapped Multi- and Hyperspectral Image Fusion

Article

  * Jan 2025
  * IEEE T GEOSCI REMOTE

  * Jiaxun Li
  * Wei Wang
  * Xiaolin Han
  * WD Sun

High-spatial-resolution multispectral (HM) and low-spatial-resolution hyperspectral (LH) image fusion over the same scene has been intensively studied. However, in practical application scenarios, HM image usually covers a larger area than LH image, thus the same scene-oriented fusion framework can only be used to a limited range of the overlapping area. To solve this problem, a dictionary expansion based incompletely overlapped HM and LH fusion method is proposed here, try to expand the dictionary learned within the overlapping area to the other non-overlapping area, and then to reconstruct an entire high-spatial-resolution hyperspectral (HH) image over the area covered by the whole HM image. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The LPN progressively reconstructs the high-spatial-resolution images in a coarse-to-fine fashion by using multiple pyramid levels. Second, spectral characteristics between the low- and high-resolution HSIs are studied by the non-negative dictionary learning (NDL), which is proposed to learn the common dictionary with non-negative constraints. The super-resolution results can finally be obtained by multiplying the learned dictionary and its corresponding sparse codes. Experimental results on three hyperspectral datasets demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed method in enhancing the spatial resolution of the HSI with preserving the spectral information simultaneously.

Keywords:

hyperspectral image (HSI); super-resolution; deep Laplacian pyramid network (LPN); dictionary learning

## 1. Introduction

Hyperspectral imaging systems sample the electromagnetic spectrum of scene radiance by hundreds of contiguous spectral bands. The obtained hyperspectral image (HSI) [1,2,3,4], which has a high spectral resolution, is a data cube containing very narrow spectral bands ranging from the visible to infrared spectrum, enabling the fine representation of different land-covers by spectral signatures. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 2.2.2. Class-Adaptive Dictionary Reconstruction

The CADR process is illustrated in Figure 1. It constructs a class-adaptive dictionary for each class using a small number of labeled training samples. This dictionary is then applied to all pixels within the corresponding class to achieve sparse representation and reconstruction. This class-level modeling enables full exploitation of the shared spectral structures among pixels within the same class while avoiding cross-class interference.

(1) Class-Adaptive Dictionary Learning: Let the hyperspectral data be as follows:

X=[{x}_{1},{x}_{2},\dots ,{x}_{N}]\in {\mathbb{R}}^{B\times N}

(3)

Here, B denotes the number of spectral bands, N represents the total number of pixels, and the corresponding class labels are

y=[{y}_{1},{y}_{2},\dots ,{y}_{N}],{y}_{i}\in \{\mathrm{1,2},\dots ,C\}

(4)

For each class c, randomly select no more than {n}_{\mathrm{s}} pixels from its labeled samples to form the training sample set {S}_{c} (in this study, five training samples were selected per class), thereby constructing the training sample matrix.

(11)

where the denominator normalizes the atom to unit norm, preventing scale ambiguity. This procedure is repeated for all atoms until the maximum number of iterations is reached.

The sparse coding step and dictionary update step are alternately executed until the objective function converges or the preset maximum number of iterations is reached. Through this alternating minimization process, the final output comprises the class dictionary {\mathrm{D}}_{c}^{\prime } corresponding to each class and its sparse representation {\mathrm{A}}_{c}^{\prime } on the training samples.

(2) Class-Sparse Reconstruction: After completing class dictionary learning, fix the learned dictionary {\mathrm{D}}_{c}^{\prime } and apply it to all pixels in that class. Let the data matrix composed of all pixels in class c be

{X}_{c}^{\mathrm{all}}\in {\mathbb{R}}^{B\times {N}_{c}}

(12)

Here, {N}_{c} denotes the total number of pixels in class c.

By solving the following sparse coding problem, we obtain sparse representations for all pixels under the dictionary {\mathrm{D}}_{c}^{\prime }:

{\mathrm{A}}_{c}^{″}=\mathrm{a}\mathrm{r}\mathrm{g} \underset{A}{\mathrm{m}\mathrm{i}\mathrm{n}} {\displaystyle \frac{1}{2}}{\parallel {X}_{c}^{\mathrm{all}}-{\mathrm{D}}_{c}^{\prime }A\parallel }_{F}^{2}+\alpha {\parallel A\parallel }_{1}

(13)

Reconstructing raw data based on sparse representations:

{\widehat{X}}_{c}={\mathrm{D}}_{c}^{\prime }{\mathrm{A}}_{c}^{″}

(14)

Here, {\widehat{X}}_{c}\in {\mathbb{R}}^{B\times {N}_{c}} denotes the reconstructed data for class c.

Through this sparse reconstruction process, pixels within each class are constrained to be represented within the same dictionary subspace. This enhances spectral consistency within classes, suppresses outliers and noise components, and provides the classifier with more stable and discriminative feature representations.


(19)

Here, \mathrm{Y}\in {\mathbb{R}}^{N\times C} represents the one-hot encoded class label matrix, and \lambda is the regularization coefficient used to suppress overfitting. The closed-form solution is efficiently computed as

\beta ={\left({\stackrel{~}{\mathrm{H}}}^{\mathrm{\top }}\stackrel{~}{\mathrm{H}}+\lambda \mathrm{I}\right)}^{-1}{\stackrel{~}{\mathrm{H}}}^{\mathrm{\top }}\mathrm{Y}

(20)

where \mathrm{I} denotes the identity matrix. To enhance the numerical stability of the model on hyperspectral data, this paper adapts the regularization parameter based on the conditional properties of the feature matrix.

#### 2.2.4. Environment Configuration

The hardware configuration for this experiment includes an Intel Xeon processor, 128 GB of RAM, and an NVIDIA RTX A4000 GPU, which satisfies the computational requirements for HSI data processing and model training. The experimental code is implemented based on Python 3.8. NumPy (v 2.2.6) and SciPy (v 1.15.3) are mainly used for numerical calculations and file input and output operations. Scikit-learn (v 1.7.2) is adopted for dictionary learning and data normalization, while PyTorch (v 2.4.0+cu121) is employed to construct the data loading pipeline. Matplotlib (v 3.10.8) and Seaborn (v 0.13.2) are utilized for visualization of the results, which ensures the reproducibility and scalability of the experiment. For reproducibility and future research, the code and associated experimental resources of the proposed method are publicly available at the GitHub repository: https://github.com/wllnHUOT/CADR-BL.git (accessed on 10 April 2026).
